place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 药园 · 这一年
place.en: Chending Temple · The herb garden · That year

setup.zh: 马小宝押了七回没押着，告到执事房：沈小满送人的丹，九道纹；药园是他巡的。周衡翻开巡夜簿：「药园，一株不少。要告他偷，拿赃来。」
setup.en: Seven bets and not one win; Ma Xiaobao goes to the stewards' office: the pills Shen Xiaoman gives away have nine rings, and he patrols the herb garden. Zhou Heng opens the night-watch book: "The herb garden — not one plant short. If you accuse him of theft, bring the stolen goods."

recap.zh: 马小宝告你偷了药园的灵草，周衡翻开巡夜簿：「药园，一株不少……要告他偷，拿赃来。」又问孙二狗那颗丹几道纹——「我看了」。阿禾拿本子上马小宝那七笔押注、你正月十九下山那一行，请钱掌柜钉出一块「头彩一颗　已开」，只在你那一页记了一行：头彩一颗，利息另算。清明替外公烧了纸。一晃五年，第三年阿禾先筑了基，观主袖子里的丹；祁长松也筑了基，第五年腊八你规规矩矩赢了大比，观里那颗一转的官丹，揭了封，米汤粘回去，进了饭桶；入秋，九层大圆满。
recap.en: Ma Xiaobao accused you of stealing from the herb garden; Zhou Heng opened the night-watch book: "The herb garden, not one plant short… if you accuse him of theft, bring the stolen goods." Then he asked how many rings Sun Ergou's pill had — "I looked." A-He laid Ma Xiaobao's seven bets and the line "nineteenth of the first month, Shen Xiaoman went down" from her notebook on Shopkeeper Qian's scale pan, and a board went up — "one top prize, paid"; on your page she wrote one line: one top prize, interest charged separately. At Qingming you burned paper for Grandfather. Five years went by; in the third, A-He laid her Foundation first, on a pill from the abbot's sleeve; Qi Changsong laid his, and at Laba in the fifth year you won the contest plainly; the temple's one-turn pill, its seal lifted and glued back with rice water, went into the Rice Tub; by autumn, layer nine, great perfection.

en: "The herb garden — not one plant short."
"If you accuse him of theft, bring the stolen goods."

story.zh:
往后残株一个月一篮，篮子一年比一年浅，两三个月才出得一颗。

马小宝去坊市钱掌柜的摊子上一押三十两，押了七回，连一颗一道纹的也没押着。押到第七回，他不押了。他去了执事房。

「周师兄，」他当着一屋子领灵石的人道，「沈小满送人的丹，九道纹。钱掌柜这辈子没开过头彩，这是他自己赌咒说的。一个大比时才四层的，一开春便是五层，还一包一包的丹送人——药园是他巡的。」

这话有人信。一个四层打进了宗门大比的决赛，全观嘀咕了一冬，没人说得清他是怎么打的；如今他又一包一包往外送丹，药园又是他巡的——偷了园里的灵草炼丹，倒比押中头彩说得通。不到天黑，内门的饭堂里也在说这件事了。

周衡没有抬头，把巡夜簿翻开，一页一页往后翻，翻到末了，道：「药园，一株不少。残株是我给的，一个月一篮，账上有。」他合上簿子，看着马小宝：「要告他偷，拿赃来。」马小宝没有赃。他站了一会儿，走了。

人散了，周衡却叫住小满，把账簿往胳膊底下一夹，低声问了一句：「孙二狗那颗聚气丹，几道纹？」

小满道：「他吃得急，没顾上看。」

周衡看着他，道：「我看了。」他没再说什么，走了。往后残株照旧一个月一篮，他再没问过一个字；可每回递篮子，他都要多看小满一眼。

周衡挡得住一个「偷」字，挡不住一屋子的嘴。第二天，内门饭堂里那句话换了个说法：偷没偷不知道，沈小满手里有丹，好丹。这一句，比「偷」字要命。山上九层卡了十年八年的人，比丹多；比他高的人，也比丹多。

过了三天，坊市逢集。阿禾一早下了山，挤到钱掌柜的摊子跟前，把半文钱放在秤盘上，道：「问一句话。你这儿，出过九道纹的聚气丹没有？」

钱掌柜的手在算盘上停了一停，道：「我这儿只出一道纹。」

阿禾点点头，像是一笔账对上了。她却不走，从怀里摸出小本子，翻开一页，摊在秤盘上，拿那半文钱压住。那一页记的是马小宝：二月十九，三十两；二十，三十两；二十二，三十两……七行，一行不落，末了一个总数：二百一十两。

「三天前，」阿禾道，「马少爷在执事房，当着一屋子领灵石的人说：钱掌柜这辈子没开过头彩，是钱掌柜自己赌咒说的。」

钱掌柜的算盘不响了。

阿禾道：「马家老爷为一颗筑基丹，卖了蒙山三成的树。他要是听说，儿子二百一十两，押进了一个从来不出头彩的罐子——」她没往下说，把本子翻过一页。那一页上只有一行：**正月十九。沈小满下山寄家信，过坊市。**

「这一天，」她道，「掌柜的开没开过头彩，掌柜的自己记得。」

钱掌柜看着那一行字，看了半晌，拿指头拨了一颗算盘珠子，又拨了回来，道：「姑娘这本账，记得好。」

阿禾收起本子，转身便走。走出去三步，钱掌柜在后头道：「姑娘手里要是有九道纹的，我出五十两收。」阿禾头也不回：「不卖。」

下一个集，钱掌柜摊子顶上那块「明码标价，童叟无欺」底下，多钉了一块小木牌：**正月十九　头彩一颗　已开。**坊市里的人围着看了半天，都说钱掌柜赌的咒不算数，到底是开过的；那一天押宝的，排到了街口。马小宝又下山押了三回，三回都没押着，再没进过执事房。内门饭堂里那句话，过了半个月，也没人说了——押中头彩的漏勺，不稀奇；稀奇的是钱掌柜也有赔钱的一天。

阿禾的本子上，一个假字也没有。假的那一句，是钱掌柜自己钉上去的。

那天夜里，她翻到小满那一页，记了一行：**头彩一颗。利息另算。**
story.en:
After that the culls came one basket a month, the basket shallower every year, and a pill only every two or three months.

Ma Xiaobao went to Shopkeeper Qian's stall in the market and staked thirty taels a time, seven times, and did not win so much as a one-ring pill. After the seventh, he stopped. He went to the stewards' office.

"Brother Zhou," he said, before a roomful of people come for their spirit stones, "the pills Shen Xiaoman gives away have nine rings. Shopkeeper Qian has never paid out a top prize in his life — he swore it himself. Layer four at the contest, layer five come spring, and packet after packet of pills to give away — and he's the one who patrols the herb garden."

People believed it. A layer-four had fought his way into the final of the sect contest, and the whole temple had muttered about it all winter — no one could say how he had fought; now he was handing out pills by the packet, and he was the one who patrolled the herb garden. Stealing the garden's spirit herbs to make pills made better sense than a top prize. Before dark they were talking of it in the inner court's dining hall too.

Zhou Heng didn't look up. He opened the night-watch book and turned it page by page to the end, and said: "The herb garden — not one plant short. The culls I give him, one basket a month; it's in the books." He shut the book and looked at Ma Xiaobao: "If you accuse him of theft, bring the stolen goods." Ma Xiaobao had none. He stood a while, and left.

When the people had gone, Zhou Heng called Xiaoman back, tucked the ledger under his arm, and asked, low: "Sun Ergou's qi pill — how many rings?"

Xiaoman said: "He ate it in a hurry. Didn't stop to look."

Zhou Heng looked at him and said: "I looked." He said nothing more, and left. After that the culls came one basket a month as before, and he never asked another word; but every time he handed over the basket, he gave Xiaoman one look more.

Zhou Heng could stop the word "theft"; he could not stop a roomful of mouths. The next day, in the inner court's dining hall, the talk had changed its shape: theft or no theft, who knew — Shen Xiaoman had pills, good pills. That was deadlier than "theft". On this mountain there were more people stuck at layer nine for eight or ten years than there were pills; and more people stronger than him than there were pills, too.

Three days later was market day. A-He went down the mountain early, squeezed up to Shopkeeper Qian's stall, put half a cash on the scale pan, and said: "One question. Has anything from this stall ever come out as a nine-ring qi pill?"

Shopkeeper Qian's hand stopped on the abacus. "My stall only gives one ring."

A-He nodded, as if one sum had come out right. But she didn't leave. She took out her little notebook, opened it to a page, spread it on the scale pan and weighed it down with the half cash. The page was Ma Xiaobao's: nineteenth of the second month, thirty taels; twentieth, thirty taels; twenty-second, thirty taels… seven lines, not one missing, and a total at the bottom: two hundred and ten taels.

"Three days ago," said A-He, "young master Ma stood in the stewards' office before a roomful of people come for their spirit stones and said: Shopkeeper Qian has never paid out a top prize in his life — he swore it himself."

The abacus went quiet.

A-He said: "Old master Ma sold three tenths of the trees on Mengshan for one Foundation pill. If he hears that his son put two hundred and ten taels into a jar that never pays a top prize —" She did not go on. She turned the page. On it was a single line: **Nineteenth of the first month. Shen Xiaoman went down to send a letter home; passed through the market.**

"That day," she said, "whether you paid out a top prize or not — you'll remember that yourself."

Shopkeeper Qian looked at the line for a long while, flicked one abacus bead over with a finger, flicked it back, and said: "The young lady keeps a fine set of books."

A-He put the notebook away and turned to go. Three steps off, Shopkeeper Qian said behind her: "If the young lady has a nine-ring one in hand, I'll pay fifty taels for it." A-He didn't turn her head. "Not for sale."

By the next market day, under the board that said "Fair prices, no cheating young or old", a new little board had been nailed to the stall: **Nineteenth of the first month — one top prize — paid.** People in the market stood round it a long time and said Shopkeeper Qian's oath didn't count after all, he had paid one out; that day the queue to bet reached the end of the street. Ma Xiaobao went down and bet three more times, won nothing three times, and never set foot in the stewards' office again. Within half a month nobody in the inner dining hall was saying it any more — a leaky ladle hitting a top prize was nothing much; Shopkeeper Qian losing money for once, now that was news.

In A-He's notebook there was not one false word. The false line was the one Shopkeeper Qian had nailed up himself.

That night she turned to Xiaoman's page and wrote one line: **One top prize. Interest charged separately.**

exits.means: the spring: burns paper for his grandfather facing Mengshan; A-He's strip of rice by the herb-garden wall, fed with her own qi (they drink more than the herbs); she swallows her nine-ring pill there — layer seven, short of what it should give, the rice gone nearly black-green overnight

story.zh:
清明那天，他在后山寻了一块向着蒙山的石头，替外公烧了一沓黄纸——外公的坟在镇上，他去不了。他念着他娘教的口诀，念到「五居中央」，纸烧完了，灰飞起来，打着旋儿往山下去。

那天傍晚，他去药园东角寻阿禾。观主派她照看药园，说木天灵根，拿一园子药草练手；她每天在园里，他每夜巡园，两个人一天总要碰上两回。她在东角墙根底下拔了一溜杂草，空出巴掌宽的一条地，没跟谁说。开春她启了竹筒上的蜡，把禾种倒出来，种了下去，出了二十来棵，一棵一棵地黄。她便夜夜把手按在土上，拿自己的气喂它们。一园子的药草，她喂惯了，喂完一畦，额头上见一层汗；这二十来棵禾，她要喂到后半夜，脸白得跟窗户纸一样。禾不黄了。

小满蹲在她旁边看了一会儿，道：「它们喝你的气。」

阿禾道：「喝得比一园子药草还多。」她把手收回来，在衣襟上擦了擦，「坡田里长的，饿惯了。」

那颗九道纹的聚气丹，她一直揣着。那天夜里，她蹲在地头把它吞了，一只手按着土，坐到天亮。天亮的时候，她是练气七层了。这样一颗丹该冲多远，她在藏经阁里查过，心里有数——差了一截。墙根底下那二十来棵禾，一夜之间，绿得发黑。
story.en:
On Qingming he found a rock on the back hill facing Mengshan and burned a stack of yellow paper for Grandfather — Grandfather's grave was in the town, and he could not go. He recited the formula his mother had taught him; as he reached "five in the middle", the paper burned out, and the ash flew up and spun away down the mountain.

That evening he went to find A-He at the east corner of the herb garden. The abbot had put her in charge of the herb garden — a wood heavenly root, he said, could learn her hand on a gardenful of herbs; she was in the garden every day and he patrolled it every night, so the two of them ran into each other twice a day at least. Along the foot of the east wall she had pulled a strip of weeds and cleared a palm's width of ground, and told nobody. In spring she broke the wax on her bamboo tube, shook out the rice seed and sowed it; twenty-odd shoots came up, and one by one they yellowed. So every night she pressed her hand to the soil and fed them with her own qi. The herbs of a whole garden she was used to feeding — a bed done, and a film of sweat on her brow; these twenty-odd stalks she had to feed till past midnight, and her face went as white as window paper. The rice stopped yellowing.

Xiaoman squatted beside her and watched a while, and said: "They're drinking your qi."

"More than a whole garden of herbs," said A-He. She took her hand back and wiped it on her jacket. "Grown on hillside fields. They're used to going hungry."

The nine-ring qi pill she had kept on her all along. That night she squatted at the head of the strip and swallowed it, one hand pressed to the soil, and sat till dawn. At dawn she was at Qi Refining layer seven. How far a pill like that ought to carry you she had looked up in the scripture library, and she knew — it had come up short. Along the foot of the wall, in a single night, the twenty-odd stalks had gone a green so deep it was nearly black.

label.en: The dog days · Five years go by

exits.means: the hot months: nights on the herb-garden wall with A-He and Sun Ergou — then five years: layers six to nine in a few lines, and three short scenes — Qi Changsong, Foundation laid, flies his sword into the same east-corner cypress the pig talisman once rammed him into (the kitchen auntie: poke or not?); in year three A-He, fifteen, lays her Foundation on the abbot's pill from his sleeve, hidden, and teases him with interest; at Laba in year five he goes up again after four years away, Shopkeeper Qian lists him at one-pays-fifty, A-He's single cash is the only stake on him; five bouts won plainly by small wits (the north wind, the half-stick rule), Qian counts out fifty-one cash to her; the sect's one-turn pill resealed with rice water into the Rice Tub; five brides on the Zhang

refuse.zh: 一季一季来：先过了前头那一季。
refuse.en: One season at a time: finish the one before first.

story.zh:
伏天里最热的那几夜，药园巡完了，三个人常坐在药园的矮墙上乘凉：小满，阿禾，孙二狗。

小满问：「你想叫什么？」孙二狗想了半天，道：「……还叫二狗吧。我娘叫惯了。」

小满没笑。阿禾也没笑。墙底下的小狰翻了个身，打了个响鼻。

一晃，便是五年。

看官，凡人修仙，最不值钱的是日子。越往上越慢，一层爬上一两年是常事；一届百来个进山门的，练到九层大圆满的，不过三五个。

沈小满这五年，一年一层：六层，七层，八层，九层；七层上卡了大半年，他也不急。秘境里那一撮土，在他丹田里长成了一块厚地，吸一口，存一口；饭桶吐出一颗九道纹的，他吃一颗，那口缸便深一截。他睡着以后，木牌里那只爪子，还在他身子里一下一下地凿。瞿老不许他下山：「没筑基，别下山。在你家门口站过一夜的那个人，等的就是你下山。」家信一年两封，他娘的字仍旧又小又密：屋顶不漏了；你爹的膝盖，阴天疼，晴天也疼；吴婆婆的牙，还在。内门的屋子一间也没空出来，他仍旧睡在大通铺最靠门的那张铺上。大比年年比，头几年，他不上台——那颗丹，九层大圆满才吃得，他拿了也只能揣着，倒招一观的眼睛。

祁长松转过年开春便出了关，筑了基。一转的丹，十个里冲得过三四个，他是那三四个里的一个；观里便改口叫他祁师叔。

筑了基的，便踩得剑。祁师叔头一回踩剑，是一个大清早，外门的人正在演武场上做早课。后山那边先起了一道青光，歪歪斜斜，忽高忽低，像一只喝醉了的燕子。近了，众人才瞧清剑上站着一个人，方脸，两只脚死死钉在剑脊上，钉得跟当年钉在那道拼缝上一模一样——可剑不是石头，脚钉得越死，剑越不听使唤。那剑在演武场上空兜了一个圈子，兜到东角，「哗啦」一声，一头扎进了那棵老柏里。

演武场上一百来个人，没一个敢笑出声。就是那一棵。前年腊八，一张画着猪的黄纸，拉着他撞上去的，也是这一棵。

伙房大娘拎着晾衣杆跑出来，跑到树底下，仰脸一瞧，是祁师叔，那根杆子便举不上去了：「……师叔，捅不捅？」树里静了一会儿，柏枝里头传出祁长松的声音，还是那么平：「捅。」

捅了三下，才捅下来。祁长松落了地，拍掉一身的柏叶，把剑插回鞘里，一抬头，瞧见了人堆里的小满。他看了一会儿，道：「你那张猪，还有没有？」小满道：「……没了。」祁长松点点头：「可惜。它飞得比我稳。」说完，背着手走了，一步一步，走得极慢，脚底下踩得极实。

那一天，外门背着人笑了一整天。小满没笑。东角那棵老柏的树皮上，新撞掉了一块，白生生的，挨着前年撞掉的那一块。一个人等一颗丹，等了二十年，等到了，头一回飞，落在树上。他自己呢，还在练气的半山腰上。他在肚里算了算自己还要等几年，没算下去。

五年里的第三个秋天，阿禾十五，《阴符经》头一篇「生」，读到了头。观主把她叫进正殿后头的静室，从袖子里摸出一只小瓷瓶，倒出一颗丹，搁在她手心里，道：「今夜，吃了。」没有大比，没有名录，周衡的账上，也没有这一笔。她挑的是个没月亮的夜，锅盖云扣在正殿顶上，天是黑的，云也是黑的，全观没一个人抬头。观主在静室门外坐了一夜，天亮进去看了她一眼，只说了一句：「出了这扇门，你还是练气。」一个十五岁的天灵根筑了基，传到太一宫的耳朵里，她便不是沉鼎观的人了。

第二天傍晚，小满巡园巡到东角，照例在矮墙上坐下。阿禾蹲在那几棵禾跟前，手按着土，头也不回，道：「我筑了。」

小满道：「筑了什么？」话一出口，他自己便懂了。她还是那个背影，两根辫子，一件洗白了的袄；可他往她身上一看，从前看得见的那一点气，看不见了，像一盏灯，给人罩上了灯罩。

他先出来的是一声笑，真笑，笑得从矮墙上跳了下来：「真的？」阿禾道：「昨夜。」小满道：「疼不疼？」阿禾想了一想，道：「疼。比你大比那天疼一点。」

他还在笑，笑着笑着，心里有一处地方，轻轻抽了一下。大比那天他在台上一场一场地打，打得肋骨一抽一抽地疼，那只玉盒子到底是人家的；她那一颗，是从袖子里摸出来的。他知道这不怪她。他也知道，这一下抽，不是假的。

阿禾回过头来，看了他一眼。她看人一向准，这一眼也准。她把手从土里拿出来，在衣襟上擦了擦，一本正经地道：「我先上去，替你看看上头什么样。哪一级滑，哪儿有坑，一样一样记下来，等你上来，交给你。」顿了一顿，「收利息。」

小满道：「多少？」阿禾道：「还没算。你上来得越晚，利息越多。」

小满又笑了。这一回，一半是真笑，一半是认了。那天夜里，他在柴房里把贴肉揣着的那个油纸包打开，九道金纹，透亮得像一滴凝住的露水，全天下也找不出几颗——可它说不清来历；她那一颗，说得清。他七层，吃不得。他看了一会儿，一层一层包了回去，吹了蜡烛，在黑地里小声道：「……利息，少算一点。」

每年除夕，周衡都要去一趟正殿；每年从正殿出来，都说一句：「明年，弟子再来。」观主每年都是那一句：外门里，今年没人筑基。只有第三年，周衡在殿里站得久了些，观主多给了半句：「亲传，不算外门。」每年十月十八，周衡一整天不翻账簿，巡夜的蜡烛，也不掰了。小满不问。

秦雁第二年进了内门，第五年上，筑了基。孙二狗两年一层，爬到了三层，爬上一层，便在大通铺门口哭一回。阿禾那一小条地年年种，年年多半是瘪穗。小满这几年学的，也不只是层数：褚先生那几样五行的法术，他五门挨个儿练了个遍；邹青松那只赤铜葫芦，他关起柴房的门，拿自己的火气一丝一丝地喂；瞿老一个月两回，在崖顶上拿扫帚把教他巽四的剑。

那一年腊月，钱掌柜照旧把板子扛上了山，在老槐树底下支开摊子。板上头几行，仍旧是内门的；最底下一行，写的是：**沈小满　一赔五十。**

有人问：「九层了，还一赔五十？」钱掌柜拨着算盘道：「五门伪灵根拿头名，三百年没出过。五门伪灵根的九层，跟单灵根的九层，不是一个九层。」又拨了一下，「四年没上过台。全观记得的沈小满，是四层的、浑身是血、倒挂在树上的那一个——九层的他出手，谁见过？我没见过。没见过的，我往大里写。」

阿禾挤到秤盘跟前，放下一文钱。钱掌柜抬起眼皮：「姑娘，五年前你押过他一回。」阿禾道：「输了。」钱掌柜道：「还押？」阿禾道：「他四年没上台，我没处押。」接了纸条，揣好，走了。那一年押沈小满的，统共一文钱。

第五年腊八，刮的是北风。头一场，小满抽着的是内门一个火行的九层。他上了台，头一件事不是看人，是看演武场边上那面旗——旗往南扯。先看风，后看鹿；身后没人替他说，他自己说。他往北边那块青石板上一站，便不挪了。那师兄的火弹一颗接一颗打过来，他拿土墙接，接一颗，碎一面，满台是烟；烟顺着北风，全往南倒，倒进那师兄自己的眼睛里。那师兄咳一声，退半步，咳到第七声，退到了台边。小满这才走过去，伸手推了一把。掉下台的，输。

中间三场，一场靠脚，一场靠数，一场靠对面那人自己急了，没一场打得好看。决赛的对手，是内门一个九层大圆满，等那颗丹等了九年，一上台便是全力，金刃一道接一道。小满躲得开的躲，躲不开的挨，挨一下，往后犁出半尺，脚底下那块厚地照旧稳着；他不大还手，只是一口一口地吐，吐得比吸的长。半炷香烧到了底，执事看谁占着上风：那师兄扶着膝盖，喘得像一头拉了一天磨的驴；小满站着，额上有汗，气是匀的。执事的锣槌在手里转了两转：「沈小满，胜。」

这一回没有猪蜻蜓，也没有镜子，五场，一场一场打下来，打得规规矩矩，台下的人都说没意思。周衡把那本蓝布面的名录翻到新的一页，提起笔来，写了「沈小满」三个字，笔停了一停——三百年的名录上，头一回写一个五门伪灵根的名字。观主把玉盒子放在他手里，封条上盖着大印。

钱掌柜在老槐树底下收摊。阿禾把那张纸条摊在秤盘上，一个字也没说。钱掌柜抬头看了一眼板子顶上那块「已开」的小木牌，叹了一口气，解开布袋，一文一文往秤盘上数：「一，二，三……」数得极慢，一文一声响。数到二十，围上来七八个人；数到四十，围了一圈。小满站在她身后，跟着那一声一声的响，在肚里一文一文地数。数到五十，钱掌柜的手在袋口停了一停，又摸出一文，搁在最上头：「本钱。」

阿禾把五十一文拢进帕子里，摸出小本子，翻到五年前那一页。那一页上还是那一行：**一文。利息另算。**她在底下添了一行：**五十一文。利息另算。**

钱掌柜把板子往肩上一扛，走出两步，又回过头来，冲小满背上那张弓一抬下巴：「那木头，打听出名字没有？」五年，他年年腊月扛板子上山，见了小满，头一句都是这一句。小满道：「没有。」钱掌柜道：「不急。」

当夜小满在柴房里揭了封条，盒盖一开，一股药气又苦又腥；一道纹，纹边两三点黑斑，一转，下品；饭桶闻了一口，满脸嫌弃，炉盖一合，再不理他。他讨了半碗米汤，把封条粘了回去，连玉盒子塞进饭桶肚里——全天下唯一一颗他拿出来说得清来历的筑基丹。

这五年，漳水边上，每年十月十八，推下去一只船，船上坐一个穿嫁衣的姑娘。五年，五只船。沉鼎观离漳水十天的路，观里没有一个人知道她们叫什么。周衡知道是哪一天。
story.en:
On the hottest nights of the dog days, when the garden round was done, the three of them would sit on the herb garden's low wall to cool off: Xiaoman, A-He, Sun Ergou.

Xiaoman asked: "What would you like to be called?" Sun Ergou thought for a long time and said: "…Ergou still. My mother's used to it."

Xiaoman did not laugh. Nor did A-He. Under the wall the little Zheng rolled over and snorted.

Five years went by in a blink.

Reader, in mortal cultivation days are the cheapest thing there is. The higher you climb the slower it goes — a year or two for a single layer is common; of the hundred-odd who come through the gate in one intake, three or five reach layer nine, great perfection.

Shen Xiaoman's five years: one layer a year — six, seven, eight, nine; he was stuck at seven for most of a year and did not fret. The pinch of earth from the secret realm had grown into a field of thick soil in his dantian: one breath in, one breath kept. Each nine-ring pill the Rice Tub gave up, he ate, and each one made the jar a little deeper. Once he slept, the claw in the token was still at work inside him, chipping, stroke by stroke. Old Qu would not let him go down the mountain: "No Foundation, no going down. The man who stood a night at your door is waiting for exactly that." Letters came twice a year, his mother's hand still small and dense: the roof doesn't leak now; your father's knee hurts when it's overcast, and when it's clear too; Granny Wu's teeth are still there. Not one inner-court room came free, and he still slept in the bunk nearest the door. The contest came round every year; the first few years he didn't go up — the pill was for layer nine, great perfection; he could only have carried it about, and drawn the whole temple's eyes.

Qi Changsong came out of seclusion the very next spring and laid his Foundation. On a one-turn pill three or four in ten get through, and he was one of the three or four; the temple took to calling him Uncle-Master Qi.

Once you have laid your Foundation, you can ride a sword. Uncle-Master Qi's first ride was early one morning, while the outer court was at morning practice on the training ground. Over the back mountain a green light rose, slanting, now high, now low, like a drunken swallow. As it came near they made out a man standing on the sword, square-faced, both feet nailed to the blade's spine exactly as they had once been nailed to that seam in the stone — but a sword is not a stone, and the harder the feet were nailed, the less the sword obeyed. It swung one circle over the training ground, swung to the east corner, and with a great rustle went headfirst into the old cypress.

A hundred-odd people on the training ground, and not one dared laugh out loud. That tree. The Laba before last, a yellow paper with a pig drawn on it had dragged him into that very tree.

The kitchen auntie came running out with her laundry pole, ran to the foot of the tree, looked up, saw it was Uncle-Master Qi, and could not raise the pole. "…Uncle-Master — poke, or not?" Silence in the tree for a while; then out of the cypress boughs came Qi Changsong's voice, as level as ever: "Poke."

Three pokes, and down he came. Qi Changsong landed, brushed off a coat of cypress needles, slid the sword back into its sheath, looked up, and saw Xiaoman in the crowd. He looked at him a while, and said: "That pig of yours — have you any left?" "…No," said Xiaoman. Qi Changsong nodded. "Pity. It flew steadier than I do." And he walked off, hands behind his back, step by step, very slowly, each foot set down very firm.

All that day the outer court laughed behind people's backs. Xiaoman didn't laugh. On the bark of the old cypress at the east corner a fresh patch had been knocked off, raw white, right next to the patch knocked off the Laba before last. A man waits twenty years for a pill, gets it, flies for the first time, and comes down in a tree. And he himself was still halfway up the slope of Qi Refining. He started to reckon how many years he had left to wait, and did not finish the sum.

In the third autumn of those five years A-He was fifteen, and she came to the end of "Birth", the Scripture's first chapter. The abbot called her into the quiet room behind the main hall, took a little porcelain bottle from his sleeve, tipped out a pill and laid it in her palm. "Tonight. Eat it." No contest, no register; and in Zhou Heng's ledger, no entry either. She chose a moonless night; the pot-lid cloud sat over the main hall's roof, the sky was black and the cloud was black, and not one person in the temple looked up. The abbot sat outside the quiet room all night; at dawn he went in, looked at her once, and said only: "Once you're out of this door, you're still Qi Refining." A fifteen-year-old heavenly root who had laid her Foundation — let that reach the Taiyi Palace's ears, and she would no longer be Chending Temple's.

The next evening Xiaoman's round brought him to the east corner, and he sat down on the low wall as usual. A-He was squatting by her few stalks, hand on the soil, and without turning her head she said: "I've laid it."

"Laid what?" said Xiaoman — and the moment it was out, he understood. She was the same back as ever, two braids, a jacket washed pale; but when he looked at her, the little glow of qi he had always been able to see was gone, like a lamp someone had put a shade over.

What came out of him first was a laugh — a real one; he laughed himself right off the wall. "Truly?" "Last night," said A-He. "Did it hurt?" said Xiaoman. A-He thought about it. "It hurt. A bit more than you, the day of the contest."

He was still laughing, and somewhere in the middle of it something in his chest gave a small pull. On the day of the contest he had fought bout after bout on that platform till his ribs throbbed with every breath, and the jade box was someone else's in the end; hers had come out of a sleeve. He knew it wasn't her fault. He knew, too, that the pull was not a pretend one.

A-He turned and gave him one look. She read people well, and she read this well too. She took her hand out of the soil, wiped it on her jacket, and said, perfectly straight-faced: "I'll go up first and see what it's like up there for you. Which step is slippery, where the holes are — I'll write it all down, and hand it over when you get there." A pause. "With interest."

"How much?" said Xiaoman. "Haven't worked it out," said A-He. "The later you come up, the more interest."

Xiaoman laughed again. This time half of it was a real laugh, and half of it was owning up. That night in the woodshed he opened the oilpaper packet he carried against his skin: nine golden rings, clear as a drop of frozen dew, not many like it under heaven — but it couldn't say where it came from; hers could. At layer seven he couldn't take it. He looked at it a while, wrapped it back up layer by layer, blew out the candle, and said softly into the dark: "…Go easy on the interest."

Every New Year's Eve, Zhou Heng went to the main hall; every year he came out and said, "Next year I'll come again." Every year the abbot said the same thing: nobody in the outer court has laid a Foundation this year. Only in the third year did Zhou Heng stand in the hall a little longer, and the abbot gave him half a sentence more: "A personal disciple isn't outer court." Every year on the eighteenth of the tenth month Zhou Heng did not open his ledger all day, and did not break his night-watch candle in half. Xiaoman did not ask.

Qin Yan entered the inner court the next year, and in the fifth year she laid her Foundation. Sun Ergou climbed a layer every two years, up to three, and every layer he climbed he cried once at the door of the long bunk. A-He sowed her strip of earth every year, and every year most of the ears were empty. Nor was it only layers Xiaoman learned in those years: the few five-element spells from Master Chu's lecture hall he worked through, all five doors, one by one; Zou Qingsong's red-copper gourd he fed, behind the barred woodshed door, with his own fire, wisp by wisp; and twice a month on the clifftop Old Qu taught him the sword of Xun Four with the handle of a broom.

That year in the twelfth month Shopkeeper Qian carried his board up the mountain as always and set out his stall under the old locust tree. The first few lines on the board were inner court, as ever; the very last line read: **Shen Xiaoman — one pays fifty.**

Someone asked: "Layer nine now, and still one pays fifty?" Shopkeeper Qian worked his abacus. "A five-door false root taking first — not once in three hundred years. A five-door false root's layer nine and a single root's layer nine are not the same layer nine." Another flick. "Four years and he's not been up on the platform. The Shen Xiaoman the whole temple remembers is the one at layer four, covered in blood, hanging upside down in a tree — him at layer nine in a fight, who's seen that? I haven't. What I haven't seen, I write long."

A-He squeezed up to the scale pan and put down one cash. Shopkeeper Qian lifted his eyelids. "Young lady, five years ago you bet on him once." "I lost," said A-He. "Betting again?" said Shopkeeper Qian. "Four years he hasn't gone up," said A-He. "I had nowhere to bet." She took her slip, tucked it away, and left. That year, the whole stake on Shen Xiaoman came to one cash.

At Laba in the fifth year the wind was from the north. In the first bout Xiaoman drew an inner-court fire-root at layer nine. He got up on the platform, and the first thing he looked at was not the man but the flag at the edge of the training ground — it streamed south. Wind first, then the deer; there was no one behind him to say it, so he said it himself. He stepped onto the northern slab and did not budge. The senior's fireballs came one after another; he took them on earth walls, one wall smashed for each ball, till the platform was all smoke; and the smoke went with the north wind, all of it south — into the senior's own eyes. The senior coughed once and gave half a step; by the seventh cough he had backed to the edge. Only then did Xiaoman walk over and give him one push. Off the platform, you lose.

Three bouts in the middle: one won with the feet, one with counting, one because the man across from him lost his patience — not one of them pretty to watch. The final was against an inner-court layer nine, great perfection, who had been waiting nine years for that pill, and who came out at full strength, metal blades one after another. What Xiaoman could dodge he dodged; what he couldn't, he took — each one ploughed him back half a foot, and the thick ground under him held as ever. He hardly struck back; he only breathed out, breath after breath, each out-breath longer than the in. The half stick of incense burned down, and the steward judged who had the upper hand: the senior was bent over with his hands on his knees, panting like a donkey that has turned a mill all day; Xiaoman stood there, sweat on his brow, his breath even. The steward turned the gong-stick twice in his hand. "Shen Xiaoman wins."

This time there was no pig-copter and no mirror: five bouts, fought one after another, by the rules, and the crowd below all said it was dull. Zhou Heng turned the blue register to a new page, took up his brush, and wrote the three characters Shen Xiaoman, and the brush paused — in three hundred years of the register, the first time it held the name of a five-door false root. The abbot laid the jade box in his hands, the seal stamped with the great seal.

Shopkeeper Qian was packing up under the old locust tree. A-He spread her slip on the scale pan and said not a word. Shopkeeper Qian glanced up at the little board above his stall that said "paid", sighed, untied his bag, and began counting onto the scale pan one cash at a time: "One, two, three…" — very slowly, one clink to a coin. By twenty, seven or eight people had gathered; by forty, there was a ring of them. Xiaoman stood behind her and, clink by clink, counted along in his belly. At fifty, Shopkeeper Qian's hand stopped at the mouth of the bag; then he took out one more cash and laid it on top. "Your stake."

A-He gathered the fifty-one cash into her handkerchief, took out her little notebook, and turned to the page from five years ago. On it was still the one line: **One cash. Interest charged separately.** Beneath it she added a line: **Fifty-one cash. Interest charged separately.**

Shopkeeper Qian swung the board onto his shoulder, went two steps, turned back, and jerked his chin at the bow on Xiaoman's back: "That wood — found out its name yet?" Five years he had carried his board up the mountain every twelfth month, and every year, seeing Xiaoman, that was the first thing he said. "No," said Xiaoman. "No hurry," said Shopkeeper Qian.

That night in the woodshed Xiaoman lifted the seal; the lid opened on a smell both bitter and rank: one ring, two or three dark flecks beside it, one-turn, low grade; the Rice Tub sniffed it once, pulled a face of disgust, shut its lid, and would have nothing more to do with him. He begged half a bowl of rice water, glued the seal back down, and tucked it, jade box and all, into the Rice Tub's belly — the one Foundation pill in all the world whose history he could tell.

In those five years, every eighteenth of the tenth month, a boat was pushed out on the Zhang with a girl in a bridal gown sitting in it. Five years, five boats. Chending Temple was ten days from the Zhang, and no one in it knew their names. Zhou Heng knew which day it was.

exits.means: the autumn month: the lake brims over, layer nine, great perfection; his master calls him up the cliff

refuse.zh: 一季一季来：先过了前头那一季。
refuse.en: One season at a time: finish the one before first.

story.zh:
到得入秋，丹田里那口水缸满得往外直漾，吸进去一口灵气，便溢出来一口，再也添不进去了——外门的人管这个叫「九层巅峰」；褚先生的名册上，只写四个字：九层大圆满。

八月里，瞿老叫他上了一趟崖顶。
story.en:
By autumn the great jar in his dantian was brimming over: breathe in one breath of spirit and one spilled out; nothing more would go in — the outer court called this "the peak of layer nine"; in Master Chu's register it was written in four characters only: layer nine, great perfection.

In the eighth month, Old Qu called him up to the clifftop.
